children: Bitcoin and gold are moving together more closely than ever. The 90-day correlation between the two assets has reached an all-time high, which is unusual for a pair usually pitched as rivals.
For most of its life, Bitcoin traded like a high-octane cousin of the Nasdaq. Lately it has been acting a lot more like the metal its fans keep comparing it to.

By early September 2026, Bitcoin's 90-day rolling correlation with gold had climbed to between +0.56 and +0.59. According to the research, that is the strongest link between the two since at least 2017.
The previous high-water mark came during the 2020 post-COVID stimulus period. Back then, the correlation peaked at roughly 0.50 to 0.53, a level the current reading has now cleared.
The short-term view is even tighter. Over the same stretch, the 30-day correlation between Bitcoin and gold ran as high as +0.72 to +0.80.
While Bitcoin cozied up to gold, it drifted away from tech. Its correlation with the Nasdaq 100 dropped to approximately +0.30, a one-year low.

The price action tells a similar story, with a twist. After the US Treasury expanded its long-bond purchases to as much as $4 billion weekly, Bitcoin gained around 22% to 26% in August, while gold rose about 5% to 6%.
Volatility is narrowing too. Bitcoin's volatility ratio relative to gold has shrunk to approximately 1.43 to 1.7 times, down from 5.6 times in 2021.

Investors are reaching for hard assets because of the US fiscal picture. Federal debt has surpassed $40 trillion, and Treasury yields spiked, a move the research ties to the expanded long-bond purchases.

Analysts from firms including Bitwise and The Block have connected the elevated Bitcoin-gold correlation to these rising fiscal concerns. In their reading, the shared driver is worry about currency debasement and the direction of fiscal policy.

The timing of the two correlation peaks is worth noticing. The 2020 high arrived during a period of heavy stimulus, and the 2026 record has arrived amid mounting anxiety over US debt and bond-market stress.

For investors, the most direct implication is about how Bitcoin is being used. The rising correlation suggests some investors may be shifting strategies, treating Bitcoin less as a pure speculative bet and more as a hedge against economic instability and currency debasement.

The Nasdaq decoupling is the more interesting piece for portfolio builders. If Bitcoin trades separately from tech stocks, it may start appearing in defensive allocations rather than sitting in the same risk bucket as growth equities.
There is a big caveat, though. In past episodes of bond-market stress, Bitcoin's decoupling from equities has proven short-lived.

The gap in performance is another reason to be careful with the digital gold label. A 22% to 26% monthly gain sits alongside a 5% to 6% move in gold, which means Bitcoin is moving in the same direction as gold while still carrying a much bigger risk profile.

There are a few markers worth watching from here. The first is whether the 90-day correlation holds above the 2020 peak of roughly 0.50 to 0.53, which would suggest this is a regime rather than a blip.
The second is the Nasdaq 100 correlation. If it climbs back from its one-year low of about +0.30 the next time equities sell off, the safe-haven argument takes a hit.

The third is the policy backdrop itself. The Treasury's long-bond purchase program and the broader debt picture appear to be pushing Bitcoin and gold together, so any change there could undo the link just as quickly as it formed.

The last is the volatility ratio. If Bitcoin keeps closing the gap with gold, the comparison becomes harder to dismiss as marketing, and the case for Bitcoin as a macro hedge rests on how it trades rather than how it is branded.

title: Bitcoin's 90-day correlation with gold hits a record high
